extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming, testing, and appraising inductive inferences, hypotheses, and experimental methods in natural and moral sciences. Emphasizes limits of induction, legitimacy of hypotheses, and correct application of experimental methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ultimate laws of nature' are distinguished from derivative laws and from collocations; an ultimate law is not part of the constitution of things if it might possibly be terminated or altered by natural causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when assessing whether a generalization claims an irreducible, invariant law or a derivative/contingent regularity; an asserted ultimate law must be robust against conceivable natural alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of necessity in human actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying a person's actions necessarily follow from his character means that he invariably does act in conformity with his character and that one who thoroughly knew his character could predict how he would act in any supposable case — not implying Asiatic fatalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about volition and causation, prefer the weaker, predictive/invariate sense of 'necessity' (invariability and predictability) rather than metaphysical fatalism; check whether objections conflate 'necessity' with repugnant fatalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of hypothesis (test laid down)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate scientific hypothesis is one from which consequences can be deduced and compared with facts; even if initially tentative or based on slight grounds, it is justified if it is testable and can be disproved by comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge hypotheses by their capacity for empirical consequences and refutation (deductive testability). Examples: Broussais' fever-localization, Gilbert's earth-magnet hypothesis, Gall's phrenology (tentative), Darwin's natural selection (legitimate hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis must be capable of producing the same kind of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: For a unifying hypothesis to be plausible, the proposed cause should be shown to be capable of producing the phenomena in question 'according to the same law'; otherwise the unity is a mere guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing generalizations that merge distinct phenomena under one cause, require demonstration that the cause accounts for them by the same governing law (not merely superficial similarities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rules of Induction and rules of Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of Induction concern conditions of proof; rules of Hypothesis concern the legitimacy of speculative suggestions. One is not obliged to have induction-proof to propose a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an author is advancing a proven inductive claim or a provisional hypothesis; critique of a hypothesis must respect the different standards (testability, fruitfulness) from those of established induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and experiment are the ultimate basis of all knowledge for obtaining elementary laws, but experimental methods become illusory in dealing with complex combinations where causes continually change or are many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply experiments confidently for elementary or well-isolated physiological phenomena; be skeptical of simple experimental claims in complex social, political, or multifactorial contexts without careful control and deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method applicability: Agreement and Difference vs Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of Agreement and Difference are often inapplicable to complicated natural cases, but the Method of Concomitant Variations can sometimes single out influencing causes by noting antecedents whose variation is followed by variation in the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the inductive method appropriate to the case: use Concomitant Variations when causes vary and correlate with effect magnitude; do not expect Agreement/Difference to work where causes are complex or collocated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty when many influencing causes exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are many influencing causes and no one predominates, and some are continually changing, it is scarcely possible to trace a relation between variations of the effect and any one cause sufficient to assign its real share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat causal attribution with caution in multifactorial systems; avoid precise apportionment of causal shares unless one cause strongly predominates or can be isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiments are often imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural experiments where Nature imitates man's experimental types often use complex means that cannot be perfectly analyzed, making it uncertain whether the supposed cause or some unknown agency of the means produced the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural experiments only as corroboration of conclusions reached by other, more controlled methods; scrutinize the means by which the 'experiment' was effected to rule out confounding agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes (and apparent exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of Composition of Causes is fulfilled when considering immediate effects: apparent exceptions (e.g., one spark vs two, threshold doses) arise when the immediate effect is a collocation and duplication of collocation does not always double remote effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with apparent failures of compositionality, check whether the immediate vs remote effect distinction explains the anomaly; consider time/place differences and limits of effect yields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about attributing regularity to chance or providence
rubrics_metrics.description: Different thinkers interpret the evidence of design differently: some see design in laws/uniformities, others in collocations (special adaptations). One should not conflate predictability with absence of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing arguments from design or teleology, distinguish between evidence drawn from uniform laws and that drawn from special collocations or seemingly lawless events; critique should note which type of evidence is being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of explanation are limits of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific explanation and inductive generalization are identical in scope; the limits to inductive generalization are the limits to the agreement or community of facts — you cannot generalize beyond observed similarity unless the cause can be shown to produce the phenomena under the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the empirical basis for generalizations and avoid unwarranted mergers of distinct phenomena; require demonstrable community of facts and mechanism if generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for probability inference: importance of first instance and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The first instance is important because it shows possibility (presence of a cause adequate to the event); subsequent instances indicate the frequency, intensity, and invariability of the cause — we reason by referring to causes, not merely counting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In probabilistic judgments, assess whether the first occurrence established possibility and whether repeated instances indicate stability of the cause; avoid naive frequency-only inferences divorced from causal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of chance calculations when possibilities undefined
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation of chances breaks down where possibilities cannot be properly enumerated (e.g., infinite or ill-defined categories such as 'all possible colors'); without special experience or inference, setting the list of possibilities is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply simple combinatorial probability when the sample space is ambiguous; require empirical or principled basis for enumerating possible outcomes before applying probability formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean vs average for inductive inquiry (least squares principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive inquiry the 'mean' is not the arithmetical average when deviations are asymmetric; the most probable determination of invariable elements is that which minimizes the sum of the squares of the individual deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate central tendency measures (e.g., least-squares estimation) rather than naive arithmetic means when inferring invariant elements from observations, especially when outliers are unevenly distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental verification in social/political contexts needs prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated observed sequence (e.g., announcement of diplomatic rupture followed by money-market derangement) is inconclusive as an experiment; it can only verify a deduction if we already understood the motives or mechanisms connecting the events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require theoretical or historical grounding before treating single historical coincidences as causal evidence in political/economic domains; corroborate with multiple, well-documented cases and deduction from known motives/mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of speculative but testable conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold speculations (e.g., brain as voltaic pile, natural selection) are legitimate if they are testable and capable of being rendered disprovable or probed by consequences — they may open fruitful lines of inquiry even if initially unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speculative proposals by their empirical consequences and capacity to guide further investigation; tolerate provisional inadequacy if the hypothesis is promisingly testable and theoretically fertile.
